Recent papers report that the frequency of major outages in large cloud provider WANs has remained roughly constant over the years.
There is a vast literature on increasing network availability through testing, emulation, and formal verification.
Almost all such existing approaches aim to prove that an output is correct given a particular input, e.g., a configuration or set of values, and do not focus on validating the input itself.

Techniques such as verification, replication, testing, and similar methods validate a system's output assuming correct inputs, so their guarantees are rendered meaningless when the inputs to the system themselves are incorrect.
Even extensive pre-rollout testing cannot catch all bugs before deployment because the wide range of configurations, network loads, and OS versions makes such testing infeasible.
The Evolve or Die paper extracts learnings from more than 100 outages at Google.
It includes examples of outages due to incorrect inputs but does not report incorrect inputs as their leading cause.

The difference from the authors' analysis may be because it looked across both SDN- and protocol-based WANs, is nearly a decade old, and some of its recommendations may now be common practice leading to new dominant causes.
Flexible Contracts for Resiliency provides a language for reasoning about chains of assumptions that connect ground-truth signals to higher-level abstractions.
Anomaly detection approaches detect outliers in input data through statistical analysis of a signal's past history.
These approaches focus on outliers in a signal's history rather than on whether the signal reflects ground truth, which requires corroboration across signals.
Network operators today maintain detailed network models that can describe router-level signals.
Traffic demand information can be collected from measurements at end hosts rather than from routers directly, as in bandwidth-allocation systems.
Routers can run simple applications that can issue active probes to check link status.

Root-cause studies of production network and cloud infrastructure consistently find that configuration errors, management actions, and software bugs in control/management systems cause a large fraction of service-impacting outages.

Public-cloud outage studies similarly attribute many incidents to software and configuration issues rather than to physical data-plane failures, showing that maintaining correct control-plane state remains a significant operational challenge.
Centralized WAN controllers make forwarding and traffic-engineering decisions from a global model that includes live topology and traffic-demand measurements.
If an input such as topology or demand does not reflect the current network, the controller can compute an incorrect plan even though its optimization and control logic is functioning correctly.
Network verification research checks a given snapshot of forwarding or configuration state for invariants such as reachability and loop freedom in real or near-real time.

Such verifiers use the controller's own state as the object of analysis; they validate policy conformance of that state but do not validate whether the state was derived from inputs that accurately reflect the live network.

Interdomain routing studies show that incorrect operator intent in the form of configuration mistakes is a longstanding cause of route failures and can be hard to distinguish from legitimate behavior until the erroneous state has already affected the control plane.
Verification and testing of SDN controller programs focuses on logical bugs in controller code under an abstract model of network events.

These techniques assume the controller receives accurate signals about topology and state, so they do not address upstream pipelines that mutate, delay, or lose those signals before the controller consumes them.
Large-scale probing and network-telemetry systems give operators an independent view of live data-plane behavior such as losses, latency, and discarded packets.
These observability systems are operated as monitoring and debugging overlays rather than as continuous validators of the inputs on which SDN control decisions are based.
A system called PROW was introduced in 1969 to accept program specifications written in predicate calculus, generate algorithms, and create LISP implementations.
Efforts by Balzer and Soloway advanced automatic programming and identified potential methods for achieving it.
Recent automatic-programming approaches use natural language processing techniques.
LLM-based agents have advanced automatic-programming development.
ReAct and Reflexion use chain-of-thought prompts to generate reasoning trajectories and action plans with LLMs.
The two approaches demonstrate that a ReAct-style loop of reasoning is effective for empowering automatic programming.
ToolFormer and ToolLLM can learn to use external tools through simple APIs.
One role-play framework for programming involves communication between agents playing different roles.
Another framework utilizes multiple agents for software development.

The role-play and multi-agent software-development frameworks have not fully exploited effective workflows with structured output formats, which makes it harder to deal with complex software engineering issues.
The broader meta-programming line of work has also included code models such as CodeBERT and recent projects such as CodeLlama and WizardCoder.
LLM-based agent systems tend to oversimplify the complexities of real-world applications.
They struggle with effective, coherent, and accurate problem solving when collaborative interaction is important.
Many LLM-based multi-agent works improve problem-solving abilities by integrating discussions among multiple agents.
Stable-Alignment builds instruction datasets from consensus on value judgments reached by LLM agents in a sandbox.
Some works on LLM agents focus on sociological phenomena, such as Generative Agents, which creates a town of 25 agents.
NL-SOM uses agents with different functions interacting through multiple rounds of mindstorms to solve complex tasks.
A cost-reduction model combines large language models as tool makers with small language models as tool users.
Some LLM multi-agent works address cooperation and competition in planning and strategy and propose LLM-based economies, focusing on open-world human behavior simulation.
LLM-based agents face pitfalls such as assistant repeated instruction and infinite loops of messages.
These pitfalls become more urgent in task-oriented collaborations that require consistent and mutually beneficial interactions.
Most current LLM-based multi-agent frameworks use unconstrained natural language as a communication interface.
Communicating required information one-to-one among agents each time complicates the communication topology and results in inefficiencies.
A prior software-development agent framework, ChatDev, relies on dialogue rather than structured documents and diagrams.
Existing methods often lack a self-correction mechanism, which leads to unsuccessful code generation.
Previous work has introduced non-executable code review and self-reflection, but these approaches still face challenges in ensuring code executability and runtime correctness.
Hallucinations in LLMs can cause code-review processes to overlook errors.
Public code benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP contain function-level code tasks, unlike datasets that focus on real-world software engineering aspects.
On a seven-task SoftwareDev comparison, AutoGPT, LangChain, and AgentVerse obtain an average executability score of 1.0, failing to produce executable code, while ChatDev obtains 2.1.

In the statistical analysis on SoftwareDev, ChatDev has an executability of 2.25, consumes 19,292 tokens, generates 1.9 code files, 77.5 total code lines, 40.8 lines per code file, requires 762 seconds, and has a human revision cost of 2.5.
AgentVerse, like general-purpose agent frameworks, lacks the ability to systematically deconstruct requirements for complex software systems.

Recursive self-improvement was first informally proposed in 1965, with first concrete implementations appearing from 1987 onward and later culminating in mathematically optimal self-referential self-improvers.

More recent work recursively improves prompts of LLMs using reasoning, analogous to earlier adaptive prompt engineering in which one neural network learns to generate queries for another pre-trained neural network.

LLM-based multi-agent applications are frequently built as systems of conversational agents that exchange natural-language messages; AutoGen is a canonical framework for such conversations, and ChatDev instantiates the idea for collaborative software development.

In these conversation-centric designs, the agentic state is carried by the message history rather than by a structured external artifact, so false or off-topic content from an early turn can be propagated to all later agents.

Several frameworks address the weaknesses of fully open-ended dialogue by imposing process structure: ChatDev organizes role-played chat along a software-waterfall lifecycle, and MetaGPT uses standardized operating procedures that assign concrete intermediate deliverables to roles.

MetaGPT explicitly motivates this structured decomposition as a way to reduce the cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies that arise when LLM-based agents are simply chained through unstructured dialogue.

A complementary body of work tries to improve the reliability of individual LLM outputs through multi-agent debate or self-refinement: independent LLM agents that read and critique each other's answers improve factuality and reasoning, and prompting for divergent multi-agent debate yields similar gains.

Self-refinement methods allow a model to revise its own generations from feedback, and Reflexion extends self-improvement by maintaining verbal self-reflections over episodes; these protocols nonetheless reason over unconstrained natural-language hypotheses rather than executable or formally checkable artifacts.

In code generation, execution has become an important feedback signal: CodeT samples candidate programs and generated tests and selects the candidates that pass those tests, while Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug shows that a model can repair code after reading compiler errors and unit-test failures.

These execution-guided methods are defined for a single code generator operating on self-contained programming problems, and they do not provide a runtime-verification protocol for multi-agent teams producing repository-scale code.

Benchmarks that approximate real, long-horizon agent use confirm the remaining gap: AgentBench evaluates LLM agents across diverse interactive environments and shows that even the best models underperform substantially on tasks that require many steps and tool interactions.

At the repository level, SWE-bench measures models on real GitHub issues and reports very low patch-success rates; SWE-agent adds an agent-computer interface for browsing, editing, and running tests, which improves performance considerably but still leaves most repository-level software-engineering tasks unresolved.

Existing datacenter congestion control algorithms are fundamentally limited to one of two dimensions when updating their congestion window or rate: they react either to the absolute network state (voltage) such as bottleneck queue length, delay, ECN, or loss, or to variations of the state (current) such as the RTT gradient.
CUBIC, DCTCP, and Vegas are examples of voltage-based CC algorithms that react to absolute properties, while TIMELY is an example of a current-based CC algorithm that reacts to the RTT gradient.
Because they are limited to a single dimension, existing schemes cannot distinguish scenarios that differ in the other dimension, which leads to reactions that are either too slow or an overreaction.
Voltage-based CC algorithms are more likely to be stable but are fundamentally limited in reaction time; current-based CC algorithms detect congestion faster but face greater stability challenges.
Voltage-based CC is oblivious to the queue buildup rate while current-based CC is oblivious to absolute queue lengths, so each class may either under-react or overreact.
TIMELY, a current-based CC deployed at Google datacenters, turned out to be unstable and was succeeded by SWIFT, a voltage-based CC.
Receiver-driven transport protocols such as NDP, HOMA, and Aeolus have been proposed and show significant performance improvements.

Receiver-driven transport relies on the assumption that datacenter networks are well-provisioned and claims congestion control is unnecessary; NDP, for example, performs no congestion control whatsoever in a Clos topology.
Receiver-driven approaches take feedback from the ToR downlink at the receiver, whereas sender-based approaches can identify congestion anywhere along the round-trip path.
Receiver-driven transport approaches make assumptions about uniformity in datacenter topologies and oversubscription.
Loss/ECN-based schemes operate by maintaining a standing queue, which does not satisfy the strict equilibrium state requirements of near-zero queue length with high throughput.
TCP NewReno flows fill the queue and then react by halving windows, causing queue oscillations; DCTCP flows oscillate around an ECN marking threshold K > b*tau/7 that depends on BDP.
Queue-length-based and delay-based (voltage-based) control laws have a unique equilibrium point.

RTT-gradient-based (current-based) control laws do not have a unique equilibrium point, so they cannot control absolute queue lengths; TIMELY in particular has been shown to lack a unique equilibrium.
ECN-based congestion control algorithms such as DCTCP, D2TCP, and DCQCN react proportionally to the ECN signal and require the bottleneck queue to grow to a threshold, which causes queuing delay.
ECN-based schemes are oblivious to congestion onset and congestion intensity.

Protocols such as TIMELY, SWIFT, CDG, and DX rely on RTT measurements for window update calculations; TIMELY and CDG partly react to delay gradients and are therefore oblivious to absolute queue lengths.
TIMELY uses a threshold to fall back to a proportional reaction to delay rather than continuing to use the delay gradient.
SWIFT, a successor of TIMELY, reacts only proportionally to delay, so it cannot detect congestion onset or intensity until the distance from the target delay grows significantly.
XCP, D3, and RCP rely on explicit network feedback based on rate calculations performed inside the network.
The in-network rate calculations used by XCP, D3, and RCP are heuristic and require parameter tuning to adjust for goals such as fairness and utilization.
HPCC introduces in-band network telemetry and significantly improves the fidelity of feedback.
HPCC's control law adjusts rate and window size solely based on observed queue lengths and lacks the control accuracy that would also account for queue dynamics.
In incast experiments, TIMELY does not control bottleneck queue lengths and loses throughput immediately after reacting to the incast.

HPCC reacts quickly and restores near-zero queue lengths after an incast, but it does not react enough during congestion onset (reaching roughly twice the buffer occupancy of a power-based scheme) and loses throughput after mitigating the incast.
HOMA sustains throughput during incasts but does not accurately control bottleneck queue lengths and retains substantially higher buffering in large-scale incasts.

Under web-search workloads, TIMELY, being current-based, does not explicitly control queuing latency, while HPCC, being voltage-based, does not react fast enough; in the evaluated setup HOMA performs worst, with short-flow flow completion times about an order of magnitude higher at high load.
HOMA's performance in this evaluation is not in line with the results reported in its original paper; recent work reports similar performance issues with HOMA.
HOMA's congestion control accuracy is limited in an oversubscribed Fat-Tree topology because congestion at the ToR uplinks cannot be controlled by a receiver-driven approach.
HOMA's original evaluation considered practically infinite switch buffers, whereas the setup here uses switches with finite buffers managed using Dynamic Thresholds.
In reconfigurable datacenter networks, reTCP instantly fills a newly available high-bandwidth circuit but incurs high latency because it pre-buffers traffic before the circuit becomes available.
In the same reconfigurable-datacenter setting, HPCC maintains low queue lengths but does not fill the available circuit bandwidth.
Research on congestion in datacenter networks includes a wide spectrum of mechanisms, such as buffer management and packet scheduling, in addition to end-host congestion control.
The dominant class of datacenter congestion-control schemes reacts to the instantaneous network state: queue occupancy, ECN marking, packet delay, or packet loss.
DCTCP uses switch-level ECN marking triggered by queue length, and the sender reduces its window in proportion to the fraction of marked packets in a round.
DCQCN carries switch ECN information to RDMA NICs through congestion notification packets and uses queue-threshold-triggered marks as the central congestion feedback.
HPCC replaces threshold marking with per-hop queue lengths and link utilization from in-band network telemetry, letting senders compute an exact current rate.
Such controls have no direct access to the rate of change of the queue signal, so their response is delayed until the absolute signal has already built or drained.
A second class of datacenter congestion control targets the variation of delay rather than its absolute level.

TIMELY is a datacenter protocol that computes the RTT gradient in the NIC and adjusts the sending rate in response to this gradient, anticipating queue growth rather than waiting for queue-level thresholds.
A control law based solely on a differentiated congestion signal has no absolute reference to the current queue length and hence no stable target at which the queue must rest.
Therefore current-only control can prevent queue growth but cannot maintain a strict near-zero-queue equilibrium across changing traffic conditions.
Datacenter protocols that do obtain near-zero queues generally replace distributed congestion control with scheduling or priority mechanisms.
Homa uses receiver-driven priorities and receiver-side queue information to schedule short flows ahead of bulk traffic, keeping queues short without a conventional sender-rate controller.

Fastpass centralizes transmission decisions in a scheduler that admits packets only when switch buffers will not form queues, providing near-zero-queue transmission at the cost of a centralized arbiter.
These scheduling-based designs are not built around the congestion-control signal classes used by sender-side protocols and require mechanisms outside the standard host transport stack.
Reconfigurable datacenter networks such as RotorNet periodically change which switch pairs are connected, exposing flows to bottleneck capacities that vary independently of host traffic demand.

The queue-threshold and RTT-gradient congestion-control protocols described above were designed for fixed-capacity network paths and do not incorporate knowledge of the timescale at which a reconfigurable link changes.

Consequently, prior sender-side controllers founded on either absolute queue state or its derivative alone cannot simultaneously deliver the fast perturbation tracking and stable near-zero-queue operation that reconfigurable datacenter workloads require.
Spot instance pricing has evolved from AWS's original bidding mechanism to more stable, diminishing-bid schemes across cloud providers.
While spot pricing is relatively stable, modeling spot instance availability is challenging because providers expose a black-box allocation system.
Prior work has attempted to model spot preemption patterns and to predict spot evictions or availability with machine-learning methods.
Bulk preemption of multiple spot instances has been observed in prior work.
A broad set of workloads—analytics, AI/ML training, HPC, and CI/CD—leverage spot instances to reduce costs.
To tolerate preemptions, these applications either checkpoint periodically and resume from the last checkpoint or re-execute the whole job.
Prior systems such as Bamboo, Spotnik, and Srifty were built for machine learning on spot instances, and CompuCache used spot instances for in-memory computable caching.
Narayanan et al. showed that using spot instances across multiple clouds can significantly reduce machine-learning training costs.
Preemptions can negatively affect application performance, and deadline-constrained applications may find it difficult to use spot instances effectively.
Preemptive execution has been studied in energy-harvesting intermittent systems, where many works schedule real-time IoT tasks under energy interruptions.
From the cloud provider's perspective, existing work has investigated maximizing revenue and enhancing runtime guarantees.

Earlier user-side studies explored bidding-based policies for deadline-constrained bag-of-task jobs on spot instances, but those policies are less applicable to today's spot markets because the pricing model changed.

Snape mixes spot and on-demand instances for long-running services and targets SLOs on the number of available instances, which differs from deadline-sensitive batch jobs that may remain idle as long as they finish by their deadline.
To the authors' knowledge, existing methods did not address switching between spot and on-demand instances in a cost-optimization and deadline-adherence setting for batch jobs.
Some cloud applications are delay-sensitive and require a job to finish by a given deadline, for example machine-learning model development.
Empirical studies of public-cloud spot markets show that spot prices are not transparent market prices; they are generated by hidden reserve-price levels that change abruptly over time.

The same empirical evidence shows that the dynamics of spot prices differ across instance types and regions, so a user cannot infer future spot availability from a single global model or from a short price trace.
Fault-tolerant dataflow frameworks recover from the loss of a worker by tracking lineage and recomputing lost partitions from surviving data.

Such lineage-based recomputation provides the task-level re-execution resilience needed by many batch workloads on preemptible instances, but it gives no upper bound on completion time when preemptions are frequent.
Deadline-aware autoscaling for cloud workflows minimizes cost by choosing the number and type of VMs to rent for the workflow while meeting a user-specified completion deadline.
Analytical bidding studies for cloud spot markets aim to select a bid that optimizes expected job cost or completion time on preemptible instances.

These lines of prior work model the workload as a finite batch or workflow whose constituent tasks can be scheduled and restarted; they do not provide guarantees for stateful, deadline-sensitive applications that must make continuous progress during each scheduling window.

Most existing concurrency control protocols execute requests based on arrival-FIFO-order and handle conflicting operations only after they have arrived or executed, missing opportunities to avoid conflicts by planning ahead.
Most concurrency-control techniques operate within the implicit constraint of arrival order and deal with conflicts as they appear.
Existing techniques that address the schedule explicitly do so only by assigning a schedule based on arrival order or by reordering the schedule after transaction commit and/or abort.

Recent work schedules transactions more intelligently by using full read-write access sets in deterministic databases or predicted key accesses, but for efficiency considers only a small subset of the schedule space such as partitioning workloads on hot keys or randomly deferring requests, resulting in suboptimal decisions.
Deterministic databases schedule batches of requests explicitly; many use FIFO order, while some improve schedules by partitioning workloads based on hot keys.
More recent scheduling proposals predict hot keys and probabilistically delay requests, or learn abort patterns, instead of systematically searching the schedule space.
Concurrency-control mechanisms generally do not proactively control the sequence in which individual operations complete and do not treat the transaction schedule as a first-class component.

Systems that do enforce schedules incur high costs, either by serializing all requests in a single thread or by requiring developers to manually construct custom rendezvous points to coordinate dependencies.
MVTSO assigns each transaction a unique timestamp corresponding to its serialization order, exposes uncommitted writes, and aborts transactions whose writes would violate the order of earlier reads.
MVTSO assigns timestamps in arrival order and does not delay later-scheduled transactions from executing before earlier ones, causing unnecessary aborts even though it enables high concurrency.
MVTSO imposes minimal execution constraints to ensure serializability compared with pessimistic locking such as two-phase locking.
Optimal transaction scheduling is NP-complete, so exhaustive search for the best schedule is infeasible in practice.
Many greedy scheduling algorithms exist in the scheduling literature, but they are not designed for transactional workloads with complex conflict patterns.
Physical resource scheduling has been addressed in prior work, while logical execution constraints from conflicts remain a bottleneck in many transactional workloads.

Many applications and OLTP benchmarks provide hot key information up front or embed it in transaction metadata, so hot key conflict patterns can be predicted from transaction type and initial arguments.
At scale, application awareness of hot keys is important for preventing one application from affecting the performance of other applications sharing the same data.
Hot-key access information can be inferred automatically from other metadata such as application stack traces and client endpoints, so explicit annotation is not strictly required.
Uniformly sampling over all possible serializable schedules for a workload is equivalent to uniformly sampling over acyclic orientations of the underlying serialization graph.

The Interval-Reversal random walk can uniformly sample acyclic orientations of an undirected graph, and nonparametric one-sided tolerance intervals provide confidence bounds without assumptions about the underlying distribution.
Most transaction-scheduling techniques focus on throughput, and a separate line of work reduces latency by scheduling transactions based on dependency-set sizes or assigned priorities.

Real-time transaction scheduling work assumes each transaction has a pre-specified deadline and focuses on minimizing missed deadlines, so it is not applicable to general DBMSs whose goal is maximizing throughput.
Transaction scheduling can be framed as an instance of the well-known job-shop scheduling problem, which has a large corpus of solution techniques.
Exact job-shop optimization methods rely on full enumeration and can be applied only to small problems, while approximation methods are used for larger problems.

Job-shop approximation methods include construction heuristics such as NEH, iterative approaches such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search, and hybrid methods, and recent work also applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to job-shop scheduling.
Modeling transaction scheduling as job-shop scheduling requires accounting for read and write operation types and for sequence-dependent execution requirements studied in some job-shop problems.
State-of-the-art job-shop scheduling search techniques find fast schedules but have very high overheads; for example, scheduling 15 transactions can take up to 30 minutes.
NEH is a known high-performing construction heuristic for minimizing makespan.
Defer, LDSF, and TS_KD[C] are prior transaction-scheduling policies that are highly dependent on arrival order and produce schedules with higher makespan and variance than a systematic search policy.

Classic concurrency-control protocols are conflict-reactive: two-phase locking and its commercial descendants block a transaction only when it requests a lock held by another transaction, whereas optimistic concurrency control aborts or restarts a transaction when validation fails.

In these protocols the order in which conflicting transactions run is determined by lock acquisition, waits, and conflict resolution rather than by any attempt to reduce the total completion time of an already admitted batch.
Practical database engines inherited this model, so the schedule of conflicting transactions emerges from lock-manager behavior and is not treated as a schedulable input.

Deterministic database systems decide an execution order for transactions before running them and replay that order across replicas to eliminate distributed deadlock detection and reduce coordination overhead.

These systems assign positions in the order through arrival timestamps or a central sequencer, and their ordering logic is constrained by deterministic replication rather than by an optimization objective for the makespan of conflicting transactions.

Protocol evaluations for main-memory databases focus on which concurrency-control mechanism to use under a given contention level, not on choosing among alternative execution orders for a set of conflicting transactions.

Makespan-minimization scheduling problems become NP-hard once precedence or resource constraints are introduced, and coloring an arbitrary conflict graph, the core decision underlying conflict-free scheduling, is NP-complete.
Because exact optimization is intractable for large instances, scheduling practice relies on greedy list-scheduling heuristics that run in polynomial time but can sacrifice schedule quality.
LLMs are autoregressive Transformer models that generate text token by token and can store computed attention states as key-value (KV) cache.

LLM inference engines typically batch requests continuously to improve throughput, but KV-cache memory can be very large: up to 800KB per token for a 13B model and up to 1.6GB for a typical 2,000-token request.
Recent work leverages prompt caching by storing attention states of frequently reused prompt segments in KV cache and reusing shared prefixes to reduce inference latency.
Cached-prompt reuse is now offered as a service by model providers at a fraction of the price of uncached prompts.
Dedicated LLM serving systems such as vLLM and SGLang provide high-throughput inference with efficient memory management and prefix-aware KV-cache scheduling.
Several optimized inference systems already reuse shared prefixes in the KV cache to reduce redundant computation.

Several systems and APIs support calling LLMs as operators over relational data, and LOTUS is an example programming framework that enables semantic queries with LLMs over tables of unstructured and structured data.
These LLM-over-tables systems provide SQL/DataFrame-style integration, but they do not explore reordering table rows and fields to optimize KV-cache hits.

Real-world relational databases exhibit repetitive data patterns, and columnar storage systems exploit repeated values across fields for compression while related techniques such as run-length encoding, multi-relational data mining, and correlation analysis use data relationships to optimize query execution.

Relational queries create data groupings based on access patterns, and techniques such as database cracking, multidimensional clustering, and Delta Lake Z-order reorganize data according to query patterns.

In the data-management community, prior work explores using cheaper ML models or probabilistic predicates to avoid running expensive inference on every row, and this line of work is orthogonal to ordering the calls to full LLMs inside a given SQL query.
Apache Spark is a widely adopted large-scale data processing engine, and Spark SQL/PySpark provide relational data processing APIs over it.
Serving systems for large language models reuse the cached attention key/value states of prompt prefixes to avoid recomputing prompt processing for repeated requests.
PagedAttention and RadixAttention provide the memory-management and cache-lookup primitives that make prefix sharing practical in general-purpose LLM serving systems.
Because key/value reuse is triggered by exact token prefixes, whether two requests can share computation is determined by the textual order in which their prompts are assembled.
Prompt Cache generalizes prefix caches by allowing an arbitrary prompt to be decomposed into application-level modules whose attention states have already been cached.

Even modular caching assumes that reusable text appears exactly as a previously cached module, so it still depends on how a relational row's values are concatenated and on which values are placed together.
A recent line of systems embeds LLM calls into SQL/dataframe query processors, making them relational-style operators over whole tables.

LOTUS provides semantic operators such as filtering, joining, and aggregating by prompting an LLM for every relevant tuple or group, while TableGPT and DB-GPT couple LLM reasoning with tables and databases.
These systems focus on operator semantics and output quality and do not consider reordering the rows or columns of the issued prompts to maximize KV-cache reuse.
Approaches that feed relational data to LLMs generally serialize each record by concatenating feature names and cell values in the order the columns appear in the input schema or dataframe.
This serialization work optimizes the text representation for semantic accuracy of a few-shot classifier or a data-understanding agent, rather than for prefix reuse in an inference backend.
Data replication and multicast have been extensively studied to optimize throughput and scalability in IP networks, peer-to-peer overlays, and inter-DC networks.
Existing throughput-optimizing techniques for multicast poorly handle the monetary cost of transfers between cloud regions and providers.
Some previous work that considers monetary cost for multicast either ignores throughput or assumes a capacity-based pricing model, whereas modern clouds charge per-GB network egress fees.
Other multicast overlay designs have used MILP formulations for optimizing throughput.

These bandwidth-based MILP formulations cannot be extended directly to per-GB costs because the cost is proportional to the product of allocated bandwidth and replication time, which would make the problem non-linear.
A significant body of prior work uses overlay networks to improve the performance and resilience of one-to-one data transfers in the Internet and peer-to-peer networks.
In clouds, previous work has also leveraged cloud elasticity to further improve transfer performance.
These prior systems do not consider the multi-destination cloud multicast problem, and except for Skyplane, none consider the monetary cost of replication in the cloud.

Skyplane's flow-based throughput model results in ambiguous multicast distribution tree solutions because it ignores the identity of data sent along multiple paths, and its optimizer cannot use multiple distribution trees to alleviate source bottlenecks.
End-system multicast and overlay multicast have been proposed to efficiently disseminate data from a single source to multiple destinations.
Application-level multicast algorithms such as SPIDER, SplitStream, Bullet, and Overcast are designed for high-bandwidth, cross-internet file distribution.
These overlay multicast algorithms ignore monetary costs and focus on techniques to maximize bandwidth.
Extensive prior work addresses inter-DC replication, including bulk multicast.
Recent research in inter-DC replication includes deadline awareness and cost awareness.
A deadline-aware inter-DC multicast scheduling and routing technique exists.
The cost model in the inter-DC setting cannot be easily adapted to cloud users because cloud network pricing is based on total data volume rather than bandwidth.
Existing inter-DC formulations are not designed for multicast or do not consider more than a few geo-distributed regions.

Traffic engineering has formulated optimization problems for minimizing cost under performance constraints, and these techniques have recently been applied to cloud providers and their monetary costs.
Entact studied how to optimize costs for online service providers while still minimizing user latency.
Cascara leveraged latency-equivalent paths to identify cost-minimizing paths for cloud providers.
These traffic-engineering approaches are developed from the perspective of the cloud or service provider and thus present a materially different optimization problem.
Without replication time constraints, a Steiner Tree minimizes egress cost, but the Steiner Tree problem is NP-hard and many approximations exist.
A Steiner Tree only optimizes total edge cost and cannot account for replication throughput or instance costs.
The Steiner Tree algorithm has been applied in the multicast setting to minimize costs in terms of delay and cloud egress costs.
CloudMPCast minimizes egress costs in cloud bulk data multicast by constructing a Steiner Tree overlay network that avoids low-throughput cross-region paths.
CloudMPCast overlooks VM capacity and per-VM egress/ingress limits in its MILP formulation.
CloudMPCast aims to achieve comparable performance to direct transfers while minimizing cost, unlike jointly optimizing throughput and cost.
Cloud services support geo-distributed storage by replicating written data from a bucket in one region to one or more buckets in other regions.
These cloud replication services have limited support for cross-cloud data movement and do not minimize egress costs even for intra-cloud movement.
SPANStore designs a system for geo-distributed storage across multiple cloud providers and optimizes egress costs of relaying data on PUT requests.
SPANStore's relay strategy is optimized for latency, not bandwidth.
The BitTorrent protocol reduces the network load on the source by allowing clients to upload and download data from each other.
P2P systems have significant overhead because they are designed for adversarial settings where peers may be unreliable or fail.
P2P systems must scale to millions of destinations and therefore lack centralized control, which prevents custom routing topologies.
P2P systems may redundantly send data over expensive links due to a lack of cost awareness.

Profiled cross-region network throughputs in clouds are relatively stable over time; prior work found throughputs stable over periods of at least 24 hours, with variations primarily across different source and destination regions.
Previous research has shown that limited numbers of overlay hops are often sufficient.
Application-layer multicast builds overlay trees or meshes to deliver data to many receivers and optimizes the overlay for aggregate throughput or end-to-end delay rather than monetary cost.
Throughput-centric overlay multicast does not model the egress fees that clouds charge when traffic leaves a region or a provider.
Peer-assisted file dissemination protocols deliberately engage the upload bandwidth of multiple helper nodes so that a single source VM is not the throughput bottleneck.

Minimum-cost multicast with network coding is formulated over capacitated links in which each link has a cost per unit of carried rate, and the task is to find a minimum-cost subgraph for a fixed multicast rate.
This capacity-based cost model is inconsistent with per-byte egress fees that vary by destination region and provider, and it does not decide throughput jointly with cost.
Geo-distributed analytics schedulers incorporate monetary cost into their data-placement and query-routing decisions.

Those schedulers are scoped to repeated analytical queries and do not address one-time bulk replication of large datasets to a user-specified set of cloud regions and providers under per-VM bandwidth caps and per-GB charges.
Prior studies have primarily profiled single-model LLM services.
Cross-model dynamics in multi-LLM serving remain largely under-examined.

Evaluations in recent multi-LLM serving work often rely on synthetic or simplified workloads, such as Poisson/Gamma arrivals, temporally rescaled traces from non-LLM domains, or dataset-driven replays.
Compute sharing has already been well studied through hardware and software mechanisms.
Effective GPU memory sharing for LLM serving remains comparatively underexplored.
Space sharing colocates multiple models on the same GPU to utilize unused memory and compute cycles.
Space sharing is effective for smaller, low-traffic models that are continuously accessed.
Time sharing swaps models in and out of GPU memory and is effective for sporadic requests because resources can be freed when models are idle.
These strategies are effective for specific cases but fail to adapt to complex and realistic multi-LLM usage scenarios.
Existing multi-LLM solutions remain fragmented, handling spatial and temporal sharing separately.
MuxServe supports spatial sharing but pins models to devices even when idle.
Aegaeon performs temporal sharing via prefill–decode disaggregation, requiring weight duplication and struggling with diverse, dynamic access patterns.

QLM time-shares GPUs by packing pending requests into groups and dispatching each group under an SLO-aware stochastic policy, swapping models and preempting unfinished requests whenever consecutive groups target different models.
QLM's frequent swapping and inefficient scheduling lead to SLO attainment lower than that of static partitioning.
ServerlessLLM unloads inactive models and reactivates a model on the server with the fastest startup based on checkpoint locality; its cold-start process dominates request latency.
Under long-tail workloads, idle models waste GPU memory.
Prior work mitigates idle-model memory waste with model eviction and accelerated weight loading.
Mainstream LLM serving engines adopt block-based KV token management such as PagedAttention.
Block-based KV cache management pre-allocates a large portion of GPU memory as a KV block pool, leaving unused memory occupied and preventing redistribution across LLMs.
vAttention and vTensor use CUDA virtual memory APIs to decouple physical and virtual memory allocation for LLM serving.
Their purpose is to simplify programming and improve kernel efficiency for single-LLM serving.
They require re-implementing a large portion of the current inference-engine stack.
SLO-aware LLM scheduling systems explore request scheduling and resource allocation to improve LLM inference performance.
These systems primarily focus on single-model serving rather than efficient multi-model serving.
GPU sharing has been extensively studied, but largely at the OS or runtime layer for application-agnostic, single-GPU workloads.
Compute-centric GPU sharing designs time-slice between latency-critical and best-effort co-tenants.
Other compute-centric approaches add preemptive scheduling across heterogeneous accelerators.
MSched is a memory-centric GPU multitasking approach that schedules GPU–CPU paging after oversubscription.
Iteration-level scheduling in LLM serving systems lets one GPU interleave tokens from many requests and suppresses the queueing stalls that appear when requests are scheduled at request granularity.
Paged cache management in vLLM keeps GPU memory under tight control during a single model's decode phase, but the parameters of every loaded model remain pinned in GPU memory.
These advances target one preinstalled LLM per serving pool and do not provide a mechanism for deciding which set of full-size models should reside in memory at any instant.
AlpaServe demonstrated that statistical multiplexing across deep learning models can reduce the GPU footprint of inference serving while still satisfying latency SLOs.
To make large models multiplexable, AlpaServe partitions a model and places its shards together with shards of other models in a common resource pool.
The model placement in AlpaServe is determined ahead of serving from profiled request rates, rather than by dynamically evicting and reactivating whole models when the popular model set shifts.
Disaggregated serving schedules prefill and decoding on separate GPU stages in order to honor independent first-token and per-token latency objectives.
Prefill-decode disaggregation is designed around the demand of one LLM or of a few high-rate LLMs and does not reclaim GPU memory occupied by many low-volume models between their bursts.
Adapter-serving systems such as S-LoRA and Punica co-locate large populations of LoRA adapters above one resident base LLM by paging and multiplexing only the lightweight adapter state.

A full-size LLM is orders of magnitude larger than an adapter delta, so the cheap paging and switching techniques used for adapter state do not directly transfer to a pool of independent full-size models.
This leaves open the core problem of fluidly trading GPU memory between active and idle complete LLMs.

Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems can handle simple dialogue tasks, but complex tasks remain difficult because naively chaining LLMs induces cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies. Real-world LLM agent frameworks tend to oversimplify the complexities of collaborative problem solving and often rely on unstructured natural-language dialogue, which loses information across rounds and produces unproductive chatter.
